newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian petrol suppliers pin hopes on U.S..
newsitem.headline: Asian petrol suppliers pin hopes on U.S..

text.p: A seasonal surge of demand in Asia is likely to reduce surplus supplies of gasoline, but some sellers are pinning their hopes on U.S. demand to remove the region's glut, traders said on Wednesday.
Traders said the seasonal tightening in export supply would underpin gasoline prices, but it would take rare incremental demand from the United States to boost prices.
Bellwether Singapore recorded gasoline stocks of 7.315 million barrels last week, near a two-year high.
Australian refiners -- normally importers -- were exporting around three cargoes in June during the southern hemisphere winter.
South Korea and Thailand turned exporters in the third quarter of 1996, as new refining capacity enabled them to export to the United States and Africa.
But the export supply could be soaked up by summer demand, traders said.

"The driving season is coming and domestic demand is increasing...we have to use most of our gasoline ourselves," said a South Korean refiner. "We are well-balanced and have no export availabilities until September."
South Korea exports about 50,000 barrels per day of gasoline.
But those exports would be diverted into the domestic market as regular demand of around 200,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) was expected to go up 40,000 to 50,000-bpd between June and August.
Supply could be further tightened by refinery run cuts in Singapore owing to weak margins.
On Tuesday sources said Esso Singapore, a recent active gasoline seller in the Singapore spot market, cut its 230,000-bpd refinery output by 10 percent.
Reforming profits have disappeared with feedstock naphtha prices currently around $2 per barrel, far below the $6-$7 break-even costs.
"Compared to the overhang in April and May, the market looks like it will sort itself out," a trader said.

But traders said gasoline prices, which have plunged more than $5 per barrel since mid-March to trade on Tuesday at $23.75, were likely to see a drastic improvement only if U.S. buying emerged to absorb Asian cargoes.
"Fundamentally, the only real demand is coming from Taiwan," said a Western trader. "In the Far East there is hardly any incremental demand...the U.S. will be the only saviour."
But some traders said it would take exceptional U.S. demand to draw barrels from Asia as historically little gasoline has traded regularly into the American market.
U.S. gasoline demand is expected to pick up in coming weeks.
